standard.title: Competitive Advantage
standard.description: processes that businesses use to create and maintain competitive advantage, including the role of entrepreneurs
standard.prior_knowledge: From Y8: how businesses adapt to market opportunities and the changing nature of work (AC9HE8K02); how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs develop market opportunities (AC9HE8K03). From Y7: entrepreneur characteristics and how these influence business success (AC9HE7K03). Students understand why businesses exist and how entrepreneurs operate but have not yet studied the specific processes used to create and maintain competitive advantage in global markets.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the processes businesses use to create and maintain competitive advantage, including the role of entrepreneurs.

nodes.label: First Nations businesses and competitive advantage
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain processes used by First Nations Australian businesses to outperform competitors and innovate in global markets, including managing cultural and intellectual property.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one process used by a First Nations Australian business to create competitive advantage (e.g. brand image, cultural IP licensing) and explain how it differentiates the business.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain the range of processes First Nations Australian businesses use to build competitive advantage: promoting brand image and uniqueness of experiences; managing cultural and intellectual property through copyright and licensing; maintaining, controlling and protecting cultural expressions in products and services (art licensing, music licensing, cultural site consulting); and collaborating through the First Nations Chamber of Commerce and Industry to share resources and build market presence.
wider: Investigate a specific First Nations Australian business operating in global markets and analyse which competitive advantage processes it uses, explaining what makes its approach distinctive
Examine how First Nations cultural intellectual property differs from mainstream IP in Australian law and explain how this shapes the strategies businesses use to protect competitive advantage
Compare how First Nations businesses in different sectors (tourism, food, art, consulting) use different combinations of the identified processes to build competitive advantage
nodes.hinge_reason: The First Nations IP and cultural property management context is substantively different from mainstream competitive advantage processes and must be treated on its own terms before students can make meaningful comparisons. Students who are taught generic competitive advantage first and then receive First Nations content as an 'add-on' develop a distorted understanding of the processes involved.

response_modes.reason: Multiple First Nations business examples across different sectors (art, tourism, food, consulting) show that the IP-protection and branding processes are adapted to different contexts, not a single formula.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations businesses operating in global markets demonstrate distinctive competitive advantage processes — particularly around cultural IP and collaborative structures — that are pedagogically rich and provide genuine comparative leverage for understanding how competitive advantage is constructed differently across cultural and economic contexts.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two processes First Nations Australian businesses use to create or maintain competitive advantage
Explains how cultural and intellectual property management contributes to competitive advantage for First Nations businesses
Uses relevant terms (e.g. 'competitive advantage', 'intellectual property', 'cultural expression')

nodes.label: Why businesses seek competitive advantage
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why businesses seek to build competitive advantage, including meeting changing market demands and improving profit margins.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two reasons why businesses seek competitive advantage (e.g. to meet competitive market demands, to improve profitability).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the reasons businesses seek to build or create competitive advantage: to meet the changing demands of a competitive global market (which shifts preferences, lowers barriers, and creates new entrants); to improve profit margins (by achieving premium prices or reducing costs relative to competitors); to sustain long-term viability in dynamic markets. Connect these reasons to the pressures businesses face in the global economy.
wider: Examine why competitive advantage is harder to sustain in digital markets (e.g. software, media) than in physical goods markets, and explain what this means for how businesses approach advantage-building
Investigate how competitor actions in global supply chains have forced Australian businesses to change their competitive advantage strategies — using a specific industry example
Analyse how shifting consumer values (e.g. sustainability, ethical sourcing) are changing the reasons businesses seek certain types of competitive advantage

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from reasoning through the competitive pressure logic: market → competitive entry → price/quality pressure → need to differentiate → processes to achieve differentiation. This causal chain makes the 'why' of competitive advantage concrete rather than a list of reasons.

success_criteria: Explains at least two reasons why businesses seek competitive advantage
Connects the reasons to conditions in competitive or global markets
Uses terms such as 'profit margin', 'competitive market', 'global market'

nodes.label: Building connections as a competitive process
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain processes businesses use to build connections that support competitive advantage, including industry collaboration, government partnerships and developing professional talent.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and explain one process businesses use to build connections (e.g. industry cost-sharing, export partnerships with government) and explain how it supports competitive advantage.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the processes businesses use to build connections that support competitive advantage: working with other businesses within the industry to share promotion costs and market access; working with government to increase exports (e.g. trade missions, export grants, bilateral agreements); developing highly skilled professionals and leaders across different industries to sustain competitive capability over time. Explain how each connection process creates advantage.
wider: Investigate an Australian industry association or export council and analyse how collective action through these bodies creates competitive advantage that individual businesses could not achieve alone

Examine how Australian universities and research institutions partner with businesses to develop human capital, and explain how this contributes to long-term competitive advantage in knowledge-intensive industries
Analyse how government-backed trade promotion programs (e.g. Austrade) support Australian businesses in building international connections, including evaluation of their effectiveness

response_modes.reason: Each connection type (industry, government, talent development) requires separate examples. Building a repertoire of specific Australian programs and partnerships — rather than treating connections generically — prepares students for evidence-based analysis tasks.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two types of connection processes businesses use to build competitive advantage
Explains how each connection type creates or maintains advantage
Uses concrete examples of connection processes in Australian contexts

nodes.label: Cost reduction and innovation processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the processes businesses use to produce goods and services at lower cost and to innovate and differentiate products and services from competitors.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one process a business uses to reduce production costs (e.g. R&D, outsourcing) and one process used to differentiate products from competitors (e.g. advertising, unique attributes).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the processes businesses use to produce goods and services at lower cost: research and development to improve efficiency; improving efficiency in development, production or delivery processes; utilising local resources; and outsourcing labour in the global economy. Explain the processes businesses use to innovate and differentiate: developing identifiable marketable attributes; using advertising and social media to build brand recognition and customer loyalty. Connect each process to how it creates or maintains competitive advantage.
wider: Investigate how a specific Australian business uses R&D investment to create competitive advantage — examining what it invests in, what outcomes it achieves, and how this compares to international competitors
Examine the ethical implications of using outsourced labour in global supply chains for competitive advantage — considering impacts on workers, communities and the business's reputation

Analyse how social media has changed the cost of differentiation for small businesses, and compare how a First Nations small business uses social media for competitive differentiation versus a multinational corporation

response_modes.reason: This node integrates all prior competitive advantage processes — First Nations approaches (Node 1), reasons for seeking advantage (Node 2), and connection-building (Node 3) — into a full picture of how businesses create and maintain advantage. Students should see cost reduction and innovation as additions to the toolkit, not replacements for earlier processes.

Cost reduction and innovation operate very differently across sectors (manufacturing vs services vs digital). Multiple sector examples prevent students from applying a manufacturing-only mental model to all businesses.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The ethical dimensions of outsourcing and the contrast between First Nations small businesses and multinationals using social media for differentiation create meaningful comparative analysis opportunities that go beyond a catalogue of processes.
success_criteria: Explains at least one process businesses use to reduce production costs
Explains at least one process businesses use to differentiate products or services from competitors
Connects each process to competitive advantage using correct economic terminology
